title: Cop31’s big fossil fuel failure
transcript:
This is the Guardian. Speaker 1: Hi, I'm Nod Haider here coming to you from Gadigal land, and this is the Full Story. Speaker 2: Global climate talks in Turkey have ended without a deal, after a standoff between oil producing states and countries demanding a more ambitious response to the climate crisis. Speaker 3: We could not, with any good conscience, support a text that effectively denies what is happening in the world and was hijacked by fossil fuel producers. Speaker 2: No mention of transitioning away from fossil fuel, that is a red line for the Pacific and we will hold on to that in the end. Speaker 1: The sticking point was language about the phasing out of fossil fuels, which was stripped out of the final draft at COP 31, where Australia's climate change Minister Chris Bowen has been leading negotiations. Speaker 3: Unfortunately, we're unable to reach agreement on a cover decision at COP. Speaker 3: And that's disappointing, very disappointing. Speaker 1: Today, Guardian Australia's environment and climate correspondent, Graham Redfern in Antalya, on how the longest climate conference collapsed. Speaker 1: It's Monday, the 23rd of November. Speaker 1: Graham, it's nice to see you. Speaker 4: Nice to see you, too, No. Speaker 1: You are in Turkey and have been following COP 31 closely over the last two weeks. Speaker 1: Can I start by getting your reaction to the breakdown of talks that have now ended without a deal? Speaker 4: So for a climate reporter, this is like your World Cup, except you don't have to wait four years in between. Speaker 4: They're every year. Speaker 4: We kind of saw this coming about three days ago, actually, but yes, today we had what they call the final plenary. Speaker 4: It started on Sunday, uh, late morning, which, by the way, is well after when the talks were scheduled to finish. Speaker 4: Uh, they still to end on a Friday, Friday afternoon. Speaker 4: So we were already way over time. Speaker 4: We were told that the talks would start at 9:00 in the morning on Sunday. Speaker 4: So we a lot of us journalists got into the media center nice and early, but the time kept shifting. Speaker 4: So they didn't get going until late morning. Speaker 4: And these United Nations conference of the parties, these cops, and this is the 31st of them, they are at times incredibly procedural and boring, and then they explode into this incredible sort of emotional torrent of activity. Speaker 4: So for the first couple of hours of the meeting, it's fairly procedural. Speaker 4: They're ticking through lots and lots, and successfully ticking through lots and lots of of different processes that are part of this, part of the United Nations framework convention on climate change. Speaker 4: But then they come to this cover decision. Speaker 4: And the cover decision is like the political deal that they're trying to make and that Chris Bowen and his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kerum, had decided this was going to be the main game for these talks. Speaker 4: They began discussing this around lunchtime, and it soon became clear that this was not going to go out they were hoping. Speaker 4: We started to get countries interjecting saying that they could not accept the text that was in front of them. Speaker 4: And because these talks work on consensus, which is isn't quite the same as unanimity, but it's similar, it became obvious quite early that this was not going to go. Speaker 4: We had some really passionate emotional interjections by the European Union, by Vanuatu, by Belize, by the Marshall Islands, by Norway, by Panama, and at that point you're looking and going, okay, this is not going to happen. Speaker 4: Now, what we've got to do is we've got to wind back a few days, because Australia released the first draft of the text for this on Monday. Speaker 4: The Monday draft was a laundry list of everything that all the 190 plus countries wanted. Speaker 4: So it's a long list. Speaker 4: There was more than 140 items on it. Speaker 4: Then we get to Wednesday and we're now down to 79 items. Speaker 4: And we're starting as journalists, we're starting to then look at the language that's being used. Speaker 4: Now, by the time the third version came out on Thursday, the words fossil fuels that had been in there before, they're gone. Speaker 4: It's just not there anymore. Speaker 4: And then by, I think it was, now you have to forgive me here because I've been awake for a long time over the last 48 hours, I had about four hours sleep. Speaker 4: But I think it was about 2:00 a.m. Speaker 4: on Sunday, we get another version. Speaker 4: There's still lots of language about carbon capture and storage, but there's still no fossil fuel language. Speaker 4: This doesn't seem to be all that much that's drifting. Speaker 4: As a journalistic group, you kind of go, well, what does that mean? Speaker 4: Now, Chris Bowen, who is the co-president of these negotiations, and again, we can talk about how he got that gig, um, all of these countries and the countries often work in blocks, they're in and out of his presidential offices in Antalya in this expo centre, constantly. Speaker 4: And it turns out that they are going in there with red lines. Speaker 4: Things that they will not compromise on. Speaker 1: So, Graham, the first draft mentioned fossil fuels, then come Sunday, there's no longer a mention of fossil fuels in the draft that was being circulated. Speaker 1: Do we know who wanted that removed and what was happening behind the scenes? Speaker 4: Of course we know. Speaker 4: We know that the petrol states, in particular, did not like that language. Speaker 4: We know that Saudi Arabia, because they spoke in the main meeting, they call it the plenary, they spoke in the plenary, they loved the language around carbon capture and storage and were mystified why people would not want that in there. Speaker 4: We know it was these kinds of countries, because to be honest, they've been doing it at COP meetings forever. Speaker 4: So you've got Chris Bowen, he's in his room, he's getting people like Saudi Arabia and the Arab group coming in saying, we're not going to compromise on this. Speaker 4: And then you have other countries coming in saying, I can't believe you're about to put out a climate pact that does not mention fossil fuels. Speaker 4: Now, this is not all that that was about. Speaker 4: There were other issues too that some of the countries were not happy about. Speaker 4: So it's things like there was not enough strong language about adaptation finance. Speaker 4: This is money to help countries to adapt to the climate change that they know is coming. Speaker 4: There've been agreements in previous cops about a tripling of adaptation finance. Speaker 4: This cop was supposed to be the adaptation cop, so they were expecting that to move and there to be some mechanisms put in place for them to access that. Speaker 4: That really wasn't articulated at all. Speaker 4: There's other language about, again, the the seriousness of climate change, particularly countries that are exposed like Pacific Island states, the low-lying islands, where for us, 1.5 degrees might be an abstract thing, but for them, it's, it's survival. Speaker 1: So the negotiations extended beyond the initial deadline.
Let's talk about Australia's role because Australia was playing a leading role in the negotiations.
You've mentioned Chris Bowen, does Australia bear any responsibility for these talks ending without a deal?
Speaker 4: I think it has to bear some. Speaker 4: And Chris Bowen was asked about this in a huge scrum, and it was a scrum outside the plenary room, while the meeting was still going on, but after he had realized that this was not going to fly. Speaker 4: He said he accepted some responsibility for what had happened, but I think also there are things that we have to understand about the way these talks are structured, that there's only so much that you can do if a bunch of wealthy, powerful countries will not shift. Speaker 4: You're kind of stuck between a rock and a hard place or in this instance, you're stuck between the EU and Saudi Arabia. Speaker 4: The EU was quite vocal in the meetings, particularly about the language around fossil fuels that they felt that as the Irish climate Minister was representing the EU voting block, Dara O'Brien said, it was unconscionable that you could have a deal without the words fossil fuels in it. Speaker 4: So he's stuck. Speaker 4: And because these processes work on consensus, there's not a lot you can do. Speaker 4: Now we heard please from other countries who spoke up in the meeting and said, we're not against this, we're not totally for it either, but we we really want people to keep talking. Speaker 4: But the clock had run down. Speaker 1: At the beginning of COP 31, Anthony Albanese faced some criticism for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech. 1: Australia is one of the world's largest exporters of coal. 1: You've spoken about the difficult bind that Chris Bowen was in as one of the negotiators. 1: Do we know much about the stance Australia took throughout this conference? Speaker 4: We know, because Chris Bowen said this after the meeting had finished, that he would have been happy to have language about a transition away from fossil fuels in the text. Speaker 4: So that's him articulating an Australian position, probably not his position as the president and the negotiations. Speaker 4: But yes, Anthony Albanese turns up early in the first week. Speaker 4: It was remarkable because he spoke only minutes after the UN Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, had given his really his last big speech on climate change before he hands over to somebody else, whoever it will be at the end of this year as Secretary General. Speaker 4: Guterres had called for developed countries to stop producing fossil fuels and selling them. Speaker 4: And then here we have Anthony Albanese coming on stage as the Prime Minister of the second largest exporter of thermal coal, the biggest exporter of meteorological coal and the country that sells 1/5 of the world's exported liquefied natural gas. Speaker 4: And then Anthony Albanese does not use the words fossil fuels in his speech. Speaker 4: When I asked Anthony Albanese in a press conference after why he'd done that, he brushed that off. Speaker 4: He said, well, there's lots of words that I didn't mention in my speech, you know, it was only a short speech. Speaker 1: But now, if we fast forward to the cataclysmic end of this meeting that we've just had, where the whole thing almost fell apart because of those two words and people's reluctance to say them, it actually tells us a lot about why those two words are important and why you have to use them. 1: And while it might not have made a difference to the climate, it was the symbol. Speaker 1: And so that's why people were so upset. Speaker 1: So, what does this bode for future efforts to tackle the climate crisis? Speaker 4: I think this may be seen as a pivot point when it comes to climate meetings and climate summits at the EU. Speaker 4: We've had some really quite big hitters in the hours since the meeting finished, who have saying we need to look at this process and reconsider it, amongst those people being Al Gore. Speaker 4: But many, many others as well, they've got problems with the consensus voting system and they've realized that you can essentially just block this process up and stop it entirely. Speaker 4: A lot of people complained that the text that was on offer to them was almost going backwards from what was agreed two years previously. Speaker 1: When we think about what was going on before this meeting, we had those incredible, awful, heart-breaking, devastating scenes in Nepal from the collapsed glacier. Speaker 1: We've got the confirmation that we're going to overshoot this temperature target. Speaker 1: We've had these incredible heat waves and fires in Europe. Speaker 1: We've got this super El Nino still building in the Pacific. 1: We've got people with food shortages in Papua New Guinea. 1: We've got Indonesia covered by fires and haze and people choking on smoke. 1: And we have a fuel crisis. 1: So when we think of all those things and we throw it all in together, and then we're in the cold light of a plenary room with some texts that weren't even mentioning fossil fuels. 1: It's not surprising that people are starting to question the process. Speaker 1: Graham, as you've described, there are positions amongst the parties that are completely unbridgeable. 1: They are diametrically opposed. 1: The US didn't even send an official delegation this year. 1: Will this mark the beginning of the end for COP? Speaker 4: I don't think it will be the beginning of the end, but I think it may start to talk about some reforms, maybe of the COP process, so that countries are not able to hold it up in the way that they have. Speaker 4: There was a moment, an incredible moment actually, where there was a press conference and the Panamanian climate Minister, Navarro, gave a speech. Speaker 4: He said, we've all got Stockholm syndrome. Speaker 5: We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia. Speaker 5: We have all been stricken by Stockholm disease. Speaker 5: We are in love with our kidnappers. Speaker 5: We love the petroleum, guys. Speaker 5: We can't live without them, and they are so smart that they have convinced us that they are actually doing this for our own good. Speaker 5: They torture us for our own good. Speaker 5: They destroy our planet for our own good. Speaker 5: They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, only limited, boundless love. Speaker 5: And we are so stupid that we fall for it. Speaker 4: It was incredible sort of off-the-cuff, but quite engaging, really powerful moment. 1: And to be honest, a lot of the press conferences at these things, they're quite bland. 1: They're talking about procedures, just transition mechanisms and and other things like that. 1: That's an important thing, but it doesn't sound like it. 1: And this guy really cut through. 1: Now, Panama sent a letter to Chris Bowen and to Turkey in the middle of the week with a whole bunch of red lines. 1: One of them was, we need to change the cop process so that this can't get held up by one country or another. 1: I think it that it's likely that we start to revisit this process. 1: Now, why don't I think this is the end for cops? 1: Because I think what cops do is they set the lowest bar possible that is expected of countries around the world when it comes to action on climate change. 1: I think setting a low bar is useful because it's the lowest expectation of what the world needs to do. 1: But I'm also not surprised that we're now seeing these other processes crop up. 1: So I think we're going to get a rich of places where climate action can take place and where countries can gather to talk about what they're going to do. Speaker 1: Graham, we appreciate you jumping on to this call with us. 1: You've been following these marathon negotiations, so we'll let you get some rest. 1: Thank you so much for your time. Speaker 4: No worries, no. Speaker 4: Thanks a lot. Speaker 1: That was Guardian Australia's climate and environment correspondent, Graham Redfern. 1: You can read more of his work on theguardian.com, and we've linked to his latest piece on the Full Story page. 1: That's it for today. 1: This episode was produced by Taylor Strano. 1: Sound design and mixing by Lou Hill. 1: The executive producer of Full Story is Hannah Parks. 1: If you like this episode, don't forget to subscribe or follow Full Story wherever you listen to podcasts. 1: And please leave us a review. 1: I'm Nod Haider. 1: Thanks for listening.
